title_patterns: [Insider group / named executive] just bought [specific unrounded dollar amount] of [N] stocks — what the filings actually show
Why insiders are [buying/selling] [SECTOR] stocks right now (the Form 4 data)
[TICKER] insider activity: [specific number] of transactions nobody covered
[N] congressional trades filed this month, ranked by size
What [specific dataset, e.g. 'every Form 4 since January'] says about [current market question]
[TICKER] earnings preview: the [N] numbers that decide the reaction
My [N]-month framework for [specific allocation decision] (with the math)
[Regulatory body] just changed [specific rule] — the mechanics for ordinary investors
hook_patterns: Open with the single unrounded figure that motivates the whole video, then state where it came from (filing, 10-Q, exchange data).
State the common assumption in one sentence, then say which data point contradicts it — no adjectives.
Name the exact source and date window up front ('these are all Form 4s filed between X and Y'), establishing that everything following is verifiable.
Lead with the question a viewer actually typed into search, then promise the answer's location in the video ('the number is at minute four').
Start by disclosing what the data cannot tell you, then what it can — credibility framing before analysis.
packaging_notes: Two duration clusters are performing: 12–22 minutes for single-topic data breakdowns, and 3–7 minutes for fast, one-question explainers. 29–33 minute long-forms only work when the topic is inherently narrative/collection-based (multiple cases stitched together).
Insider and congressional transaction data is the dominant subject cluster this cycle — it is inherently numeric and filing-backed, which suits a no-hype channel without needing sensational framing.
Specificity beats magnitude: titles naming a concrete actor, ticker or dollar figure travel further than abstract market-direction titles. Prefer unrounded numbers over adjectives.

Curiosity can be built from asymmetric information ('what the filing shows that the headline didn't') rather than from threat. Avoid the collapse/unthinkable framing visible in some outliers — it is off-positioning and unrepeatable.
Collection formats ('N stocks', 'N trades') give a clear content promise and support natural chaptering; pair with a ranked or scored structure so the payoff is explicit.
market_patterns.title: outlier pattern extraction

winning_patterns.pattern: Short-form, single-clause title: [named company/asset] + [directional move expressed as one hard number] + [short causal tag]
winning_patterns.structure: Entity → quantified move (% or price level) → 2-5 word catalyst phrase
winning_patterns.why_it_holds: The hook window has nothing to resolve except the cause, so the first seconds can pay off the number immediately. All six of our top-retaining videos were Shorts built this way, with hook-hold at or above ~1.0 and avg_view_pct clustering 66–88%.

winning_patterns.pattern: Exactly one number in the title, placed mid-title, never two competing numbers
winning_patterns.structure: One metric (either a % gain or an absolute price), not both
winning_patterns.why_it_holds: Our best-retaining Shorts each carry a single quantity; the viewer arrives with one open question. Multi-number or number-plus-qualifier titles in our set sat in the lower retention band.

winning_patterns.pattern: Congress franchise titles as [legislator name] + [buy/sell action] + [disclosure-timing clause]
winning_patterns.structure: Person → trade action → lag framing ('disclosed N days later')
winning_patterns.why_it_holds: Both congress_trade entries retained in the 66–72% range with hook-hold above 1.0 despite very small view counts. The timing clause creates a concrete, closeable question rather than a vague accusation.

winning_patterns.pattern: Catalyst named as a concrete, checkable event (a deal, a merger, a land/permit move, a named counterparty)
winning_patterns.structure: Specific noun catalyst, not a category or sentiment word
winning_patterns.why_it_holds: Our higher-retention Shorts name a verifiable event type, which matches a data-first delivery and keeps the hook promise narrow enough to satisfy in under 15 seconds.

losing_patterns.pattern: Two-clause 'skeptic twist' titles joined by a dash or 'but' that pre-deliver the debunk
losing_patterns.why_it_hurts: Both of our long videos used this shape and had the two weakest hooks in the set (hook-hold ~0.69 and ~0.74) and the only avg_view_pct figures below 60%. Giving away the punchline in the title removes the reason to stay through the hook.

losing_patterns.pattern: Appending a generic recap/date suffix after a pipe or separator
losing_patterns.why_it_hurts: The suffix dilutes the specific promise and signals a broad roundup, which appears to weaken the front-loaded hook rather than help it. Seen only on a low-retention long video.

losing_patterns.pattern: Negation phrasing ('no dollar value disclosed', 'not a signed deal') carrying the title's payload
losing_patterns.structure: Title resolves to an absence rather than a fact
losing_patterns.why_it_hurts: An absence is hard to visualise in the first seconds and leaves the hook with nothing concrete to show. Our lowest hook-hold values both sit on negation-led titles.

notes: Only two long videos in this window, both sub-60% avg_view_pct with sub-0.75 hook-hold — treat the long-form read as a flag to test, not a proven pattern. Shorts and longs cannot be compared on avg_view_pct directly because of duration.

Our top video's hook-hold above 1.0 (up to ~1.25) is replay/loop-driven within the hook window, not evidence of broad demand; its 467 views versus 145 for a structurally near-identical Short shows distribution moved independently of title shape.

market_close Shorts dominate the sample; congress_trade has only two entries at 45–66 views, so franchise-level conclusions there are provisional. These are correlations within a thin, low-view sample, not evidence that a title shape increases distribution.
